course.title: How Europe was remade
course.description: Six turning points. One connected story.

entries.title: Revolution crosses borders
entries.question: How did a revolution in France change Europe?
entries.after: French expansion and its defeat disrupted the old political order.

ideas.title: A new basis for authority
ideas.text: The French Revolution challenged inherited privilege and royal authority. Ideas about citizenship and political rights became a challenge to rulers beyond France.

ideas.title: Ideas travel with armies
ideas.text: Revolutionary wars and Napoleon’s expansion carried French power across Europe. Conquest reorganised states while also provoking resistance to French rule.

ideas.title: An empire leaves a problem
ideas.text: Napoleon’s defeat left the victors facing a geographical question: how could Europe be reorganised so that no power dominated it again?

questions.prompt: What kind of authority did the French Revolution challenge?
answer: Inherited royal authority and privilege.
Political legitimacy was increasingly debated in terms of citizens and rights.

questions.prompt: Name two ways French expansion affected Europe.
answer: It reorganised states and spread institutional or political changes.
It provoked resistance to French domination.

source.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum · Revolution to empire

entries.title: Putting Europe back together
entries.question: What were the victors trying to achieve in 1815?
entries.before: Napoleonic expansion had disrupted the European state system.
entries.after: A negotiated territorial settlement sought a balance among great powers.

ideas.title: Balance, rather than one winner
ideas.text: The Congress of Vienna reorganised Europe after Napoleon. Its architects sought a balance of power that would make another continent-dominating empire harder to build.

ideas.title: Dynasties return
ideas.text: Restoring established rulers was central to the settlement. The wishes of national movements were not its organising principle.

ideas.title: Germany remains a collection
ideas.text: The German Confederation linked 39 states, rather than creating one German nation-state. Austria and Prussia remained competing centres of power.

questions.prompt: What was the main geopolitical aim of the Vienna settlement?
answer: A balance of power: preventing one state from dominating Europe.

questions.prompt: Did Vienna create a unified Germany? Explain.
answer: No. It created a confederation of 39 states.
Austria and Prussia remained separate powers.

source.title: German History in Documents and Images · Congress of Vienna

entries.title: Many states become one
entries.question: How did Prussia change the balance of power?
entries.before: German-speaking lands were divided among multiple states.
entries.after: A German Empire emerged under Prussian leadership, excluding Austria.

ideas.title: A question of leadership
ideas.text: Unification meant deciding which power would lead. Prussia’s rise challenged Austria’s position in German affairs.

ideas.title: War changes the options
ideas.text: Victories against Denmark, Austria and France in 1864, 1866 and 1870–1871 helped Prussia establish its dominance. Unification followed a sequence of conflicts, not a single vote by all German speakers.

ideas.title: A new centre of power
ideas.text: The German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 under Prussian leadership. Austria was outside it, and a powerful new state altered Europe’s diplomatic balance.

questions.prompt: Which state led German unification, and which rival was excluded?
answer: Prussia led unification.
Austria was excluded from the new German Empire.

questions.prompt: Why did German unification matter beyond Germany?
answer: It created a powerful new state in Central Europe.
That changed the balance of power among European states.

entries.title: War breaks the imperial order
entries.question: Why did the First World War transform the map?
entries.before: Large empires ruled much of Central and Eastern Europe.
entries.after: Imperial collapse and postwar settlements produced new states and contested borders.

ideas.title: War puts states under strain
ideas.text: Years of mass warfare weakened armies, economies and political authority. Defeat and revolution helped bring down imperial regimes.

ideas.title: Four imperial orders fall
ideas.text: The Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman imperial orders collapsed during the war and its aftermath. Their timelines and successor arrangements differed.

ideas.title: New states, unresolved claims
ideas.text: Poland re-emerged and Czechoslovakia was created. New boundaries did not neatly separate populations; minorities and competing territorial claims remained.

questions.prompt: Name the four empires whose imperial orders collapsed around the First World War.
answer: Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman.

questions.prompt: Why didn’t creating new states settle every territorial dispute?
answer: Populations were mixed rather than neatly separated.
National movements and states had competing territorial claims.

source.title: US Holocaust Memorial Museum · World War I and its aftermath

entries.title: A continent divided into blocs
entries.question: How did Europe become divided after the Second World War?
entries.before: The Allies cooperated to defeat Nazi Germany.
entries.after: Rival US-led and Soviet-led blocs divided much of Europe.

ideas.title: Allies with different aims
ideas.text: After the Second World War, the United States and Soviet Union disagreed over Europe’s political future. Security fears and ideological conflict deepened their rivalry.

ideas.title: Germany becomes a fault line
ideas.text: Postwar occupation hardened into division. Two German states formed in 1949; Berlin became a particularly visible focus of the wider confrontation.

ideas.title: Alliances give division structure
ideas.text: NATO was founded in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955. Blocs shaped security and politics, though not every European country belonged to either alliance.

questions.prompt: Which two powers led the rival Cold War blocs?
answer: The United States and the Soviet Union.

questions.prompt: Name the rival alliances and one geographical example of Europe’s division.
answer: NATO and the Warsaw Pact.
Germany’s division into two states, or the division of Berlin.

source.title: Smithsonian · Origins of the Cold War

entries.title: The division comes undone
entries.question: What is the difference between 1989 and 1991?
entries.before: Communist governments and Soviet power sustained the Eastern bloc.
entries.after: Eastern bloc regimes fell, Germany reunited and the USSR dissolved.

ideas.title: Pressure for change
ideas.text: Economic difficulties, political reform and popular mobilisation undermined communist rule. Gorbachev’s reforms loosened controls without resolving the Soviet system’s crises.

ideas.title: 1989 changes the bloc
ideas.text: Communist regimes lost power across much of Eastern Europe. The Berlin Wall opened in November 1989; German reunification followed in 1990.

ideas.title: 1991 changes the state itself
ideas.text: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991 into 15 independent states. The fall of Eastern European regimes and the breakup of the USSR were connected but distinct developments.

answer: 1989: Eastern European communist regimes fell and the Berlin Wall opened.
1990: Germany reunited.
1991: the Soviet Union dissolved.

questions.prompt: Was the Eastern bloc identical to the Soviet Union?
answer: No. The bloc included separate states under Soviet influence.
The Soviet Union itself was a union of republics; its dissolution created 15 independent states.

source.title: US Office of the Historian · Collapse of the Soviet Union
